Let $f(n)$ count the number of solutions to $k\sigma(k)=n$, where $\sigma(k)$ is the sum of divisors of $k$. Is it true that $f(n)\leq n^{o(\frac{1}{\log\log n})}$? Perhaps even $\leq (\log n)^{O(1)}$?

 Building on Scott Kominers's comment, the resulting bound for \(f(n)\) can be sharpened slightly by retaining a restriction that is lost when one counts all powerful divisors of \(n\). For a solution \(k\sigma(k)=n\), let $d(k)=\prod_{\substack{p^a\parallel k\\a\geq2}}p^a$ be the powerful part of \(k\). The injection on square-free integers shows that distinct solutions in the same fiber have distinct powerful parts. Moreover, for $n>1,
n=k\sigma(k)\geq k(k+1)>k^2,
$ and hence $
d(k)\leq k<\sqrt n.
$ Therefore $
f(n)\leq Q(n):=
\#\{d\mid n:d\text{ is powerful and }d<\sqrt n\}.
$ The cutoff \(d<\sqrt n\) can then sharpen the bound, and we can derive it explicitly with Rankin's trick. For every \(s>0\),\[
\mathbf 1_{d<\sqrt n}\leq\left(\frac{\sqrt n}{d}\right)^s,
\text{which gives }
Q(n)\leq
n^{s/2}
\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\d\ \mathrm{powerful}}}d^{-s}
=
n^{s/2}
\prod_{p^A\parallel n}
\left(1+\sum_{j=2}^{A}p^{-js}\right).
\]Thus the sharp cutoff is replaced by a multiplicative weight containing a free parameter \(s\), which may then be optimized. This procedure has been called Rankin's trick because of Rankin's influential use of it in his 1938 paper on prime gaps. Taking \(s=\lambda/\log\log n\) and estimating the Euler product by the usual small/large-prime decomposition gives\[
\log Q(n)\leq
\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+M(\lambda)+o(1)\right)
\frac{\log n}{\log\log n},
\text{where}\]\[
M(\lambda)=
\sup_{A\geq2}\frac1A
\log\left(1+\sum_{j=2}^{A}e^{-j\lambda}\right).
\]Optimizing in \(\lambda\) yields\[C_0:=
\inf_{\lambda>0}\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+M(\lambda)\right)
=0.363270322648\ldots
<\frac{\log3}{3}.
\]At the minimizing value \(\lambda_0\), the supremum defining \(M(\lambda_0)\) is attained uniquely when \(A=3\). Writing \(u_0=e^{-\lambda_0}\), the critical equation is \(u_0^2+3u_0^3=3\). Consequently,\[
f(n)\leq
\exp\left(
\left(C_0+o(1)\right)\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}
\right).
\]Thus the constant in the resulting upper bound for \(f\) is lowered from \((\log 3)/3\) to \(C_0\). The constant \(C_0\) is sharp as the maximal-order constant for \(Q\), (but probably not for \(f\)). Full details, including the small/large-prime decomposition, optimization, and lower-bound construction proving sharpness for \(Q\), are available in this working paper.

 One small observation here is an improvement on the constant \(\log 2\) arising from the elementary bound \(f(n)\le\tau(n)\): 
The map \(k\mapsto k\sigma(k)\) is injective on squarefree integers; combining this with a coloring of prime-exponent patterns gives\[
f(n)\le \prod_{p\mid n}v_p(n),
\]and consequently\[
f(n)\le \exp\!\left(\left(\frac{\log 3}{3}+o(1)\right)\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right).
\]The constant \(\log 3/3\) is sharp for the maximal order of this particular majorant. (Although of course this argument does not get us anywhere close to the stronger bounds asked for in the problem.)
I have also been carrying out a bit of a computer-assisted census, and so far have confirmed that the first value with seven solutions is\[
a(7)=106345074572730040320
\]as had been conjectured at the OEIS. Moreover, \(f(n)\le5\) for every \(1<n<a(7)\), and no value of multiplicity \(6\) occurs up to \(106345074572730040320\). Together with an explicit value having exactly six preimages, this proves the somewhat surprising inequality \(a(7)<a(6)\).
Details and working notes hosted on my personal site here; comments of course welcome!

 Actually, the bound $f(n) \leq \prod_{p\mid n}\nu_p(n)$ can be proven more directly without colouring arguments - the following argument was communicated to me by Nikola Gyulev and also appeared at a team competition in Bulgaria yesterday.
Problem. Let $n = p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2}\cdots p_s^{\alpha_s}$, where $p_1 < p_2 < \ldots < p_s$ are prime numbers and $\alpha_i$, $i=1,2,\ldots,s$, are positive integers. Prove that the number of positive integers $k$ such that the sum of the positive divisors of $k$ is equal to $\displaystyle \frac{n}{k}$ is at most $\alpha_1\alpha_2\cdots \alpha_s$.
Solution. First, we note that if $m$ and $n$ are squarefree positive integers such that $m\sigma(m) = n\sigma(n)$, then $m=n$. Indeed, we have $\displaystyle \prod_{p\mid m}p(p+1) = \prod_{q\mid n}q(q+1)$, and after cancellation, consider the largest prime among the remaining prime divisors of $m$ and $n$ - without loss of generality, suppose it divides $n$. If $q\geq p+2$ for every $p\mid m$, then it is impossible for $q$ to divide the left-hand side, so by maximality the only possibility is $q=p+1$, i.e. $q=3$ and $p=2$ - but then $2 \cdot 3 = 3 \cdot 4$, which is false.
In the general case, for $\displaystyle m = \prod_{i=1}^s p_i^{\beta_i}$ consider its powerful part $\displaystyle \prod_{p_i\mid m, \ \beta_i \geq 2} p_i^{\beta_i}$. We will prove that if $k\sigma(k) = m\sigma(m) = n$ and $k\neq m$, then the powerful parts of $k$ and $m$ are different. Suppose, for contradiction, that they are the equal, and write $k = da$, $m=db$, where $a$ and $b$ are squarefree and coprime with the powerful part $d$. Since $\sigma$ is multiplicative, we have\[
d\sigma(d) \cdot a\sigma(a) = da\sigma(da) = k\sigma(k) = m\sigma(m) = db\sigma(db) = d\sigma(d) \cdot b\sigma(b),
\]whence $a\sigma(a) = b\sigma(b)$. By the first paragraph, it follows that $a=b$ and hence $k=m$, a contradiction.
We are now ready to obtain the desired bound. If $\displaystyle k\sigma(k) = n = \prod_{i=1}^s p_i^{\alpha_i}$, then $k$ divides the right-hand side. There are at most $\alpha_1\alpha_2\cdots \alpha_s$ possibilities for the powerful part of $k$, since for each $p_i$ its exponent in $k$ is one of $0$, $2$, $3$, $\ldots$, $\alpha_i$. For the remaining squarefree part of $k$, there is at most one possibility by the first paragraph. The result follows.
